title: Courage
hookLine: courage is not having no fear, but acting while afraid (Joshua 1:9)

cards: Moses is dead. The man who stood up to Pharaoh, who led the people through the sea, who spoke with God on the mountain, is gone. The job of leading the whole people across the Jordan falls on his assistant, Joshua.
Right at the start of the book that carries his name, God speaks to Joshua, and what he says, more than once, isn't a battle plan. It's a sentence meant for someone who is frightened.
Nobody tells a calm person not to be afraid.

teach.h: BE STRONG AND OF A GOOD COURAGE.
teach.b: Joshua chapter one, in the King James words: "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest."
Three things to notice. First, the command comes more than once in that chapter, the way you'd steady a friend at the edge of a high dive.
Second, God doesn't tell Joshua the danger isn't real. The river still has to be crossed, the land still entered. Third, the reason.
It isn't that Joshua is strong enough.

teach.h: THE LORD THY GOD IS WITH THEE.
teach.b: It's the LORD thy God is with thee. The courage comes from company. So in this text, courage isn't the absence of fear.

It's moving forward while afraid, because you aren't alone. Moses had said nearly the same words to Joshua before he died: be strong and of a good courage, he will not fail thee, neither forsake thee.
Then there's Esther, queen of Persia, whose people are about to be destroyed.
Her cousin Mordecai asks her to go to the king uninvited, which could cost her life: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
Her answer doesn't sound brave at all: "and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." That's courage in Esther's story. Not a cheer.
A frightened person deciding to go anyway, and asking her people to fast with her first.

how: Christians pray Joshua 1:9 and other verses of courage before surgery, exams, deployments and hard decisions, and churches tell the stories of Joshua, Esther and the saints and martyrs as examples of faith that acted while afraid.

o: trusting your own strength to win every fight
never feeling afraid when danger comes close
going forward while afraid, because you aren't alone

p: be strong and of a good courage
the LORD thy God is with thee
for such a time as this

s: God tells Joshua there is nothing to be afraid of
he tells him be not afraid, because God is with him, not because the danger is gone.
Esther went to the king because the law allowed it
she says it is not according to the law: if I perish, I perish.
the command to be strong and of a good courage comes more than once in Joshua 1
God repeats it, the way you'd steady a friend.

games.q: you're Esther. going to the king without being called could cost your life, and your people are in danger. what do you do?
o: stay silent and keep yourself safe.
ask your people to fast, then go in to the king.
send someone else in your place.
games.why: she asks her people to fast with her, then says, so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been avoiding because you're afraid, a hard conversation, a doctor's appointment, an apology, a truth you need to tell, and name the fear plainly, with no need to pretend it away.
If you pray, you can pray Joshua's verse, be strong and of a good courage, for the LORD thy God is with thee; if you don't, breathe with the fear for a minute and notice you're still here.

wordCard.voice: Courage. In Joshua and Esther, not the absence of fear, but going forward while afraid, because, the text says, God goes with them.

orig.note: Hebrew: be strong and of a good courage — God's words to Joshua.

carryVoice: Your line: brave enough. Neither Joshua nor Esther had to be fearless first. Rest well.
